utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecution versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Wednesday. I would like to greet everyone in this courtroom. I see that Mr. Scott is back with us. I'd like to greet Mr. Kruger as well, the witness, and the Defence counsel, as well as the accused. We are going to proceed with the cross-examination, and I believe that Mr. Praljak will now take the floor, because he has the lectern in front of him. Unless Mr. Kovacic starts. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Witness. The Witness would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: I just saw the witness indicating he would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Colonel. Yes. I didn't see you. You may speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to pose the following question: The attorney yesterday evening at the last part read out two rather dubious orders, and I was put in a context of having to recognise these orders or say that I should have done something about them and that I was not free to deny knowledge of them and I should have done something. I would like to read again the last pages of the minutes, if I may. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Colonel, be rest assured very often -- can't you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only hear the interpretation in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear the interpretation in German now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now I can. Now I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I was trying to put your mind at rest, because very often the witness is not familiar with the document shown to him, and that was the case with these two documents you were not familiar with. However, the Judges, as well as the parties might be interested in the tenor, in the contents of the document that the witness might be familiar with directly or indirectly. That's the reason why Mr. Karnavas put a number of questions to you with regard to the contents of these documents. And here I speak from memory, these documents were related to Zepce where the ABiH had started a military operation, and preparations had been made, and that was stated in the document. My memory's rather good, so I remember that in this document the 7th Brigade was divided up into several units that were assigned specific tasks, and after the attack it was stated that the captured persons taken prisoner were supposed to be detained. When shown these documents, you said that you were not familiar with it, but rest assured it was not a way of putting you into question. How could we do that since you were an observer there, and your only task was to observe, to monitor, because you didn't have the necessary resources to take action, to prevent any military action. That's what I wanted to tell you, and I hope that it has set your mind at rest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be allowed to respond on behalf of Mr. Karnavas, who is not here today, but I do know that he did intend to clarify the question. He'll be in today later on, but I'd like to tell the witness that it was not Mr. Karnavas's intention to put the documents to him for him to take responsibility for the fact that the ECMM didn't take any steps in that regard. The ECMM and other monitors did not know of the existence of documents of this kind, that's quite true. And I'm sure that Mr. Karnavas, when he comes into the last session today will confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Thank you very much, Ms. Tomanovic. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom and to the Colonel as well. Your Honours, for your own orientation the Praljak Defence has one hour and 30 minutes. We have been allotted 30 minutes by our colleagues Mr. Ibrisimovic, and another 30 minutes from Ms. Tomasegovic, and our original half hour which makes one hour -- one and a half hours in total. Ah, but we have further developments. 10 more minutes that was left over from my colleague Ms. Senka Nozica, which would make it an hour and 40 minutes in total, or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being told that she's used up all her time, but we'll check that. Let's not waste any time. Please proceed, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is quite possible. We'll check our arithmetic. But that would be basically the amount of time I would need. I would start off with 15 minutes, and Mr. Praljak will carry on. May we have on e-court P 9603 as our first document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you have two sets of documents. One is thicker, one is thinner. I'm going to be asking questions from the thicker documents to start off with and Mr. Praljak will do the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So anyway, Witness, the first document is this sketch that you can see on your screen. That's it. And I'd just quickly, we don't have to waste time, this is a diagram of the routes that the European observers used in Bosnia. We obtained that from one of your colleagues. And if you take a look at this, would you agree that that's what it is, of course in a schematic form, the different teams and the different areas? I think that the question can have a yes or no answer, but if anything is incorrect, you can explain that to us.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it in the form of a sketch with the borders which have been there. I don't know this, actually. I know it in a different form, but, rather, taking over the southern area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This was prepared by a colleague of yours. You might have a different diagram. And I assume that you're more familiar with the southern part, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Jablanica, Konjic, Mostar, Tomislavgrad, Livno. They're all places that you mention in your statement and testimony. So do these roads and these points on the roads more or less correspond to the area that you moved around in and not only you personally but your teams, neighbouring teams, the ECMM teams that they moved around; is that right? I see you nodding, but we need an oral answer for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: During the examination-in-chief and indeed in the statement you provided to the investigators and Prosecutor in 6312, line 6312 of the transcript, you said that you didn't move around anywhere else. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made some trips travelling to Zenica. I was also in Bugojno and Kiseljak and in Gornji Vakuf, but beyond Gornji Vakuf I didn't carry out any orders for the ECMM. These were usually journeys to Zenica, to the RC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I don't think my question was precise enough. What I meant to say was at night you didn't move around the roads; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not really what I meant. I carried out orders up to the line Prozor-Konjic towards the south, in that area, but I did travel further in the north, the purpose being to visit RC Zenica using different routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Witness. That's quite clear. But it seems that I am not asking my questions clearly enough. All I wanted to know was, and you said this, that you didn't move around at night. When the sun went down until it went up the next day, you, the ECMM, didn't move around during the night. Is that correct? I don't need any further explanations.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't conduct any operations at night, but because of the prolongation of some of our orders we were working in some time until midnight. We didn't get back to our quarters on several occasions until midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Colonel, I'd now like to ask you a few questions based on your statement that you gave to the Prosecutor. It's not actual evidence, so could you just help me out there. In your statement, in the first statement of the 18th and 19th of February, 1998, in the Croatian text it is to be found on page 3, and in the English it is on page 3 as well but higher up, and I'm going to read your exact sentence. You don't have to refer to the statement, actually. The others will be able to control me. But this is what you say: "[Previous translation continues] [In English] ... Of my tour of duty, I got totally lost and confused about the situation, and I did not had a real view on the problems that occurred in the area." Just a moment, Colonel. Could you just wait a moment to give the interpretation a chance to translate and not overlap. Now, this sentence is a quotation from your statement. It is on the record, your response to the Prosecutor, but my question in that regard is as follows: Is what you said there correct, and do you still stand by it? And then I'll go on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, and it referred to the first few days of my mandate. Fourteen days, and then I slowly found my orientation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes. Now, in that same statement, this time also on page 3. In the English it is towards the end of the page you say as follows: "[In English] Both sides always accused the other side of attacks, but it was usually unclear to us what had exactly happened." [Interpretation] So that's also contained in your statement. Now, I'll have an additional question, but please tell me whether that is indeed what you said in your statement to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say this, and this is what happened every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, further on in that same statement dated 1998, in English it is the penultimate paragraph on page 3, you go on to say: "[In English] On 16 to 18 April, clashes broke out in the whole area. It was difficult to assess the situation because everybody was shooting everyone." [Interpretation] Do you stand by that statement today?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from the date, I would put it perhaps at the 14th or 15th, but apart from that the statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, may we have document P 03554 on e-court, please, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And, Colonel, you will find the document in my folder. It is the following one, the next one in order, and it is P 03554. It's an ECMM report dated the 19th of July, 1993, and the Prosecutor showed you the same document with special reference to paragraph 8 where we have the assessments, and I'd like to look at page 2 of the English. Can you see paragraph 8 where it says "Assessment"?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Prosecutor, you answered with respect to the second portion of this section, but in fact there are two paragraphs. The second paragraph says: "No assessment on military activity [In English] is possible with only secondhand information." [Interpretation] Do you agree with that assertion?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time, and this mainly refers to Mostar, we had no access to Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So may we deduce from that in general terms that in all situations where the ECMM did not have any direct information no reliable assessments could be made about the events? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We always tried to make -- report our own findings, but often we took over reports from other organisations, but we marked them accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, to follow up on the question that was put to you, in this document that I have here in front of me you seem to acknowledge that the information related to the military situation were secondhand information. How can we explain that as part of your monitoring mission? How can we explain that you were not able to have access to Mostar? Isn't it paradoxical? You -- your mission is to monitor, but you can't observe. You can't monitor anything. And considering those circumstances, did you report the matter to your general headquarters, to Ambassador Thebault? Did you report this situation, and what was told to you? Because when you have a monitor, an observer that does not monitor or observe anything, that's not -- that's a bit of a problem, isn't?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a major problem for us, and in fact we sent reports every day that we did not have this access. This was once the case in May and then again in June also, and it lasted until July, and our superior offices including Zagreb knew about the situation but they couldn't change it. There was a memorandum of understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this memorandum of understanding that you're mentioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was a memorandum which had been agreed in 1991, I believe, with the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo, signed by President Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Kovacic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to round off this topic, Colonel, from these documents and also from the statements that you gave that we quoted excerpts from, it would appear that you had restricted or limited possibilities to observe and to gain information on the ground. Would you agree because of all the factors that we've mentioned thus far? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not in general. It was different in April, and it was different in the regions of Jablanica-Konjic, and also there was a difference between East and West Mostar. So in general terms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So am I to understand that in the following way, that in certain areas during a certain period of time, without going into details, your possibilities were limited and restricted, whereas in other areas you were able to come by information? Would that be the right way of interpreting it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And just one more document. It's the next one in my folder, P 08425. And it's a document which you compiled in your new post in 1994 during Hans Koschnik's time when you were there to implement the agreement that was reached in the meantime between the two warring parties, and I'd just like you to focus on the first paragraph entitled "Purpose." Now, Colonel, and I'll be showing you in due course a statement, an assertion that was made which you can accept or refute or comment, but anyway, from this portion I gained the impression - let's take it step-by-step - that by this document for you own team which you are team leader of in the summer of 1994, wanted to ensure by this that they gain all the necessary knowledge and information about events on the ground for them to be able to function properly. Was that your intention in preparing this document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, apart from the oral instructions this was the basic document for the monitors in this region.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Am I to understand, therefore, that you wanted to neutralise the problems which you had at the beginning of your mission in 1993 when you said that you came to the territory without the necessary knowledge beforehand? You just had a briefing, a short briefing in Zagreb and in the ministry. So did you think that this would be a tool to help you improve the situation and your understanding of it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did think so, because my instructions were, to put it briefly, rather brief, and I didn't want my successors to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would have some more questions, but since my time is brief, I'll leave them for another occasion. I apologise to the interpreters. Yes. I heard that the German interpreters hadn't finished interpreting, so I wanted to make a pause. Anyway, I think they're finished now. I don't want to take up any more valuable time. I'll leave that to General Praljak, and I can ask my questions in due course. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Colonel. Now, since we're not quite clear on whether the Croatian army was on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina or not, this hasn't been cleared up, I'd like us to go through some matters in that regard, and for that I'd like the usher to help me out and to take these two maps to the overhead projector. These are more precise maps than the ones shown you by Mr. Kovacic. We prepared them overnight. As I say, I think the maps are clearer, so would you take a look at them both on the overhead projector. Yes. Can we zoom out there to show the main roads leading into Mostar and where the individual organisations were located. Let's look at Siroki Brijeg. That's where you were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see anything for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Mostar to the right, marked with a red circle, Colonel. Siroki Brijeg. There you go. It's one of the roads leading to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only see it -- I can't see it very clearly, but as I know the area, yes, it's Mostar and Siroki Brijeg, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. Could you look further down, please. Do you see the map further south and then up, the southern section?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you pull the map up, please. Could the usher please assist me and pull the map up so we can see the bottom of the map. You see, do you agree with me we see Medjugorje there. This is a road to Mostar. SpaBat UNPROFOR were there, the European Monitors were there, the UN monitors. Is that right when I say that all these agencies were present in Medjugorje?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is accurate, but I want to say about the technology. If you ask very precise questions I would just like to point out that I can't see the places very clearly. At the moment it's not a problem because I know the area very well, but if you ask precise questions there might be technical problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you can have a look at the map that is next to you, because in your earphones you will hear the translation of General Praljak's question. So you can have a look to your right and you'll see the map much better.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel, let me ask you this: What about the border between Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, north of Metkovic, just north of Metkovici and Dracevo? There is the main road to Mostar. Was there a company of SpaBat stationed there at Dracevo, which is just north of Metkovic along the main road to Mostar? Do you remember them being there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was only in this camp once. It was a logistic base of SpaBat. I can't give any more indications than that. I can't be more precise than that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's quite sufficient, Colonel. Thank you. Could we please now place the smaller map on the ELMO, which might be easier for Colonel to use, and if I could please have an AC number for this map -- an IC number. Now, there's a smaller map, clearer for you I hope?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, we need an IC number for the map the larger one.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. That will be IC 612.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Have a look at the map, Colonel, please. Colonel, here you see the main road to Mostar, the Metkovic-Capljina-Mostar road. You also see the Ljubuski-Medjugorje-Mostar road. Further, you see the Siroki Brijeg-Mostar road. Siroki Brijeg-Mostar. It's the red dot. That's where you were. All of it. And then there's the Tomislavgrad-Vran mountain - further up towards Prozor - Road -- yes, right there. Tomislavgrad, and then across Mount Vran, up to Rama, Gornji Vakuf. If you take the road across Mount Vran, the Salvation Route as it was referred to at the time. If you look at that map, there are certain things marked on it. Do you remember that the English battalion, the UNPROFOR battalion were based at Gornji Vakuf, and at Tomislavgrad, just next to the road in Tomislavgrad, along the road itself. Is this something that you're aware of, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, and Gornji Vakuf, I also spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel, fine, thank you. We'll do the quick ones. My time's running out. So, Colonel, just this: Are you aware of the fact that the English battalion had their engineering -- Engineers Battalion at Mount Vran near the road? They helped maintain the Salvation Route as it was known at the time.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Let's not complicate matters any further. Do you know that even in Makarska and in Neum there were ECMM teams, in both Neum and Makarska that's what I'm saying it's in your documents but there's no time for me now to call them all up.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, General? ECMM you meant, you were saying?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note the microphone was off.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: I have no time to go -- to go back to the original document. Your document says that sometime in July, the European Monitors deployed both in Neum and in Makarska which is Croatian territory; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Neum, in Makarska, I was there too when passing through. In Neum I went to see the mayor, and at those times there was certainly no ECMM. At a later date, at the end of July when I left the mission, maybe then, but I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. Could you please look at P 03710. It's an OTP document. P 03710. This bears the following date: The 26th, the 26th of July, 1993. That is when you left. But you still wrote this document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't found it yet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: 03710. It's on your screen, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: One speaker at a time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right, Colonel. I'll skip the first portion, but in paragraph 2, you say: "In July '93, one team M1 Mostar and one team Split, regional centre of Knin, monitored the Croatian BiH border in the area Split-Sinj-Livno-Tomislavgrad-Posusje-Medjugorje-Neum-Makarska. Nearly all the roads, especially mountain roads which can be used by ECMM all-terrain vehicles. And then you go on to say no HV troops have been monitored. Colonel, my general question is this: Given the fact that all the roads in Herceg-Bosna were covered, all the roads leading up north by either the ECMM or the UN observers, or perhaps SpaBat or the English battalion, the fact that the Croatian border was covered by a team from Croatia, do you think any sort of movement of the Croatian army in that area could possibly have passed unnoticed? You say you noticed nothing at all, but given the sort of supervision that was in place, the system that was in place along all the roads, do you think any unit of the Croatian army could have possibly gone through without being noticed and, of course, based on the maps that I have been showing you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see anyone. That's what it says at the top of the text. Other units, UNPROFOR, thought that they had made certain observations, but it's very difficult for me to make an assessment. I've already told you that we couldn't operate at night-time. If there were major movements, then we would have seen something. That's how I would like to put it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient for my purposes. I have no time, but I'll read you a sentence. I'll ask you about that. You don't have that document. This is P 07587. This is a document produced by the UN military observers, and the date is the 15th of January, 1994. It reads: "It is very difficult to confirm the presence of any regular HV units in Bosnia and Herzegovina." When you returned to Mostar, did you have anything to indicate, some sort of additional information, please, that units of the Croatian army had been organised and fought in the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came back in June 1994, I didn't have any indications of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Do you know where Slavonski Brod is?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's in the north near to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right. Are you aware of the fact that the JNA artillery and the artillery of the army of Republika Srpska around Slavonski Brod and in the municipality, in the county, had killed over 500 civilians and dozens of children? Is this a fact that is familiar to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Germany, via the press, we got daily information during the war. I cannot recollect single incidents, and they're not my own insights but it's information gained with the press, let's say, with the newspapers or television.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. Just another question. So you watched this on TV at least. The army of the Republika Srpska and the JNA occupied a whole section of the Dubrovnik territory. They reached the sea coast. Dubrovnik itself was eventually successfully defended. Did you know that, sir? Did you have any notion of that, sir? Yes or no, sir. Don't just nod, please.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You're a professional soldier of the German army, a military man. There's one thing I want to know. When there are attacks from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina resulting in civilians being killed in a different country, according to NATO standards what would be the rights of that country in terms of defending their own civilians? We have a problem there. The JNA and the army of Republika Srpska are shelling Dubrovnik, the Slavonski Brod area, killing civilians. This is no aggression by Bosnia and Herzegovina against Croatia, but if the Croatian army go down the depth of the front tactically in order to repel the enemy, that is then termed an act of aggression by the Croatian army against Bosnia and Herzegovina. What does NATO's doctrine have to say about things like these?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, I cannot make a judgement here straight away, but of course, we would defend. If it's about our people, we would defend.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's quite sufficient. We'll probably bring that up later on in greater detail, but there is one thing that seems to be a problem here in this Tribunal. You as a soldier, would it not be clear to you that if you have the Croatian border and the enemy is repelled from the surroundings of Dubrovnik, the Croatian border cannot be defended at the Croatian border itself because the area is simply too narrow and the general lie of the land in that area? As a soldier would you not have understood that sort of thing immediately, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Operationally, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you for that question. My last question on this: Was there a single international agency there, the UN or the European Union, that provided any sort of guarantees whatsoever that they would prevent shelling and the killing of civilians, be it in Sarajevo, Slavonski Brod, Dubrovnik, or elsewhere? Was anyone at the point strong enough to provide such guarantees as to say, "You don't need to use your own army to defend your own population. We are here to provide guarantees that your population would not be attacked or indeed killed"? Were there any such guarantees provided by any of the international agencies present in the area?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, that of course did not exist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to move on to a different subject, a different subject, the situation around Konjic. Let me ask you this, sir: Reports often refer to clashes breaking out, especially when we believe that the BH army is attacking the HVO. Let me ask you this: Do you know that during the attack of the BH army against the HVO in Konjic in late March, in late March 1993, and for approximately as long as you were in the area but certainly until April at the very latest, 85 Croat civilians and prisoners of war were killed in a number of different villages, and I'm not going into the specifics as far as the villages are concerned. Are you familiar with that, sir? We only spoke about one small village, the one named Buscak.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My teammate, the Spaniard Salamanca, when he gave me a briefing in April when I arrived, he told me about that. He briefed me on that. But when I came at the beginning of April, there was a break. So it was quite calm at that moment in time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. I can't now be expected to list all the victims in April, and I don't think that's necessary. Colonel, do you know that 10.000 civilians had no choice but to leave Konjic for whatever reason? I'm not going into that now. Because of killings like these, they were forced to flee the area at the time, and there were about 10.000 of those. Were you aware of that particular partial exodus by the Croats?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about that, or I heard about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Did you what the ratio was between the forces of the HVO Brigade in Konjic and the Muslim brigades, the brigades of the BH army in the area? Did you know anything about the ratio in terms of strength between the two, the ratio, the ratio of forces between the HVO and the BH army in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would at this stage just wish to ask is this all relevant for this case. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, what is the relevance of this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance is reflected in most elements of the indictment. The indictment claims that Croats left those areas because they had been persuaded to do so by the HVO. I'm trying to take advantage of this witness's presence, the Colonel was in the area, to find out this 85 soldiers and civilians having been killed. Now, is someone leaving this area because they're facing great danger or somebody's talking them into leaving? That's one thing. Secondly, if we find out about the ratio between the HVO Brigade in Konjic and the units the BH army, we can try to find out who exactly attacked whom in that area and what their objective might have been prior to the 18th of April, 1993. So if we are familiar with the ratio then perhaps we can assume, the ratio, for example, being 1 to 6 or 1 to 5, whether an HVO brigade with a battalion, Klis battalion -- Konjic Battalion and a battalion in Klis, then all the BH army units at the time in Konjic. Your Honours, in this way we can eventually come to the general situation being discussed here. Who attacked whom in Mostar? Who attacked whom in Zenica? Who attacked whom in Travnik, in Vares? Because that is very important in terms of what the indictment claims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question put to you by Mr. Praljak as developed by him is as follows: He wants to know the ratio of forces between the HVO and the ABiH as you see it. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Konjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give any figures, but I knew and I'm also convinced that the armija forces were quite a lot stronger. I'm referring to observations at the beginning of April when I also had contacts with a brigade commander and when he told me about the situation there and the fighting.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. Could we now please go back to Mostar. Take my binder, please, and look at 3D 01015, document 3D 01015. I'll ask you the following: Do you know who Brigadier Miljenko Lasic was, the commander of the South Herzegovina operations area? Is this a name that was mentioned to you in Mostar at any time, Brigadier Miljenko Lasic?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know the Christian name, but the family name, Lasic, he was the chief of the operational unit in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. Regardless of the fact that you left on or about the 6th in purely military terms, since that's something you know about, can we please go through a number of documents that pre-date the 9th of May, 1993, the 9th of May, 1993, and then those produced after the 9th of May, and then I'll ask you as a soldier once you have we've gone through these documents. The first document the 6th of May, 1993, this is a report to the General Staff of the HVO. Paragraph number 1: "Today was quiet along the front for the most part." Then paragraph 2: "At 1530 hours at the crossroad to Nevesinje members of the BH army disarmed three civilians -- three civilian policemen and two military policemen of the HVO and took them somewhere." He then goes on to assume that these were Zuka's men were black bandannas. He says he didn't know what those people exactly were supposed to do. Did you know anything about such acts of provocation prior to the 9th of May, 1993, occurring in the area? Were you familiar with anything like that, and were you familiar with the name of Zuka?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've always heard report about such events. I know the name Zuka very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Would we please go to the following document: 3D - that's the next document in my binder - 01016. This is dated the 7th of May, 1993. Again, this is a report produced by Brigadier Miljenko Lasic to the General Staff. He says, "Exceptionally quiet night along the front line in Mostar, and then he goes on to say that four HVO combatants, three civilian, and three military policemen were taken away." He goes on to state that: "At the intersection near Lucki bridge the BH army members fired on the HVO vehicle returning from their shift. One grenade and one Zolja were fired. Eight members of the HVO were seriously wounded, and one of them eventually succumbed to his injuries. Did you know anything about this sort of incident but later, at a later stage, once you had returned?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment in time I wasn't there. I didn't get reports about such single incidents, but it was, rather, a report that mentioned such incidents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: At any rate, when you returned you probably read all the reports that had been produced based on what had been happening; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports that were drawn up by the ECMM in Mostar, yes, I did read them in -- but I don't know in how far such report would have been included in those reports. I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine, Colonel, sir. Once I've gone through these documents, and there are a number of those left, I want to ask you a very simple question. These are reports written by Mr. Lasic. Will they help us to see whether an operation was in the offing? And some people claim that this operation against the HVO by the BH army actually took place on the 9th of May. Can I have the next document 3D 01013, 3D 01013. It's a report dated the 7th of May. We can just skim through it briefly. He says that it was quiet for the most part along the front part. In Konjic, the BH forced continued to burn and loot houses. He talks specifically about the village of Seonica, attack on the village of Vrci. You say you know something about Seonica and Vrci and what happened there, or at least that's reflected in your reports. He says the situation in the town of Mostar is very complex and he says following an exchange of all prisoners of war at around 1530 hours, according to the overall principle, new arrests of HVO members and civilians followed carried out by members of the BH army. Two HVO members were arrested. One of them killed. He says that on the playground of the Tihomir Misic barracks, a single shell landed that had probably been fired by one of the BH army positions in Zalik. Let's move on to the next one, please. This is dated the 8th of May. 3D 01014. Sir, this is the next document. Can you please have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, what was the question with regard to the previous document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, I prepared -- I prepared two maps and said what my main question will be. When we get through the documents before the 9th of May and after the 9th of May, I'm going to ask this professional officer whether from these documents one can see any kind of preparation on the part of the HVO for an attack on Mostar, on the BH army in Mostar. And especially from the documents that come after the 9th of May we can see -- or, rather, we will see when we get to look at the documents, any professional can see, you included, the panic that reigned in bringing in forces to help in some sort of attack on the HVO. The Colonel is a professional soldier. I can ask him the question in general terms, and then I'll go on to specifics based on the map to see what happened there. I'm going to ask him what happened before whether he knows about that and then I'm going to ask him a basic question why everybody said the HVO did the attacking, on the basis of what documents and who was a witness to that, so I'd also like to show some video footage. I promised to show the footage when we had the witness from the -- from SpaBat in the courtroom. Another document where it says on the battlefield in the night between the 7th and 8th of May it was relatively calm, mostly it was the Serbs doing the shooting on Vranjevici. He said civilians were taken prisoner and three of our soldiers were massacred, BH forces attacking Croatian villages and so on. Let's look at the next document. Well, not the next one; I'm going to skip a few documents and look at 3D 01001. 3D 01001. It is dated the 9th of May, 1993. The report was sent out at 2000 hours, and Miljenko Lasic sets out the chronology of events, and he starts off with 1420 hours, and he says that a soldier by the name of Mario Matic was killed. And then at 1440 it says that we were informed that the Lilies, meaning the BH army, were attacking the prison of Celovina and that an order came to target the Partizan Cinema Hall. That's on the western side on -- west of the Bulevar. And then it goes on to say who was wounded. And reinforcements were requested. It says that Robert Miljko succumbed to his wounds and that the general situation in Mostar was very difficult and fighting was still going on and the HVO was trying to reinforce its positions along the Bulevar. Six defenders were killed, 17 wounded, one civilian killed, four other civilians wounded. Now, Colonel, when you returned to Mostar, did you accept this generally known fact down there that the HVO on the 9th of May attacked the BH army in Mostar, something that the international community maintained? Were you told that too?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had been told about this, too, but of course I could see with my own eyes that the staff office of the 4th Corps of the armija on the west side was burning. Obviously it had been shelled. And I heard that the 4th Corps of the armija had been moved to the east side. This was the most important thing that I was informed about on my return.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, yes, it was the staff of the 4th Corps that was in Vranica, but it says here: "The fighting is still going on. The HVO is trying to reinforce its positions along the Bulevar." Now, as a professional officer, tell me this: If the HVO is trying to entrench, to strengthen its positions along the Bulevar then how could it have launched an attack on Mostar? What kind of attack could it have launched with the existing line along the Bulevar?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would object. This calls for speculation and I think the information available to the witness, who was not there at the time, is not sufficient for him to make any assessment of this. He's not in a position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, bearing in mind the qualifications of this witness, who is a military observer, or was, I think that the question is a proper one because he is best placed to make assessments of that kind, and this was permitted with previous witnesses with the same qualifications as this one. The Prosecution on that occasion was allowed to assess the situation of troops in a village. The same question was asked, and it was asked of women that had no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me intervene in order not to waste time. You were not present on the 9th of May. We know that. Could you tell us, however, when you returned from leave? When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 25th of May of that year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You returned on the 25th of May. Were you told on your return that the HVO had attacked the HQ of the ABiH, or were you told that it was the ABiH that had attacked the HVO? Can you remember whether this was said to you on the 25th of May? Indeed this was a major event, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This changed the situation in Mostar at the time that I was there. It was a major event. The first indication was the movement of the staff of the 4th Corps of the armija to East Mostar, and it really pointed out that the HVO was the initiator rather than the armija. This was the results of the monitors. But they said especially, and let me emphasise this, we had no further access to Mostar. So from that point in time we couldn't gain our own findings and observe the situation. It was very difficult for these people. This is what they wanted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you spoke to certain individuals about these events and they did not see anything, did they, because you said that they were not present; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say precisely, but they reported that they had gained knowledge of the transfer of the 4th Corps, but after that, they had no further access to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak. You are a senior officer. Let me put a general question to you. When you have a fighting unit, military, who launch or prepare an attack, are there any orders for preparation prior to the attack? Generally speaking, in a conventional army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, such orders are always passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So I'm still speaking to a specialist. If the HVO had attacked, would there have been orders prior to the 9th of May? And if the ABiH had attacked, would there have been orders by the ABiH for the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe there would have been orders well in advance, logistic orders to do with mobilisation, transport of weapons, orders for reconnaissance troops. A whole series of orders, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, 3D 0106 [as interpreted] is the next document I'd like us to look at and see what Miljenko Lasic -- what order he's issuing. 3D 01006, on the 9th of May, 1993. This is what he says, his order: "In view of the situation in Mostar, I hereby order that 120 well-armed and trained men urgently be sent to Mostar," et cetera, et cetera. This is his order to the 1st Brigade, Knez Domagoj and to the Stjepan Radic 4th HVO Brigade as well. Then we have the Capljina Brigade and Ljubuski Brigade and he's asking that 120 well-armed men be sent out. Do we agree that that is what it says? Next document, please, which is 3D 01007, and then I'll have a general question to ask you or, rather, that is the general question. It's also a document dated the 9th of May, 1993. Once again, sent to 4th Brigade at Ljubuski and it says, "In view of the situation in Mostar I hereby order urgently to send a mortar platoon, 120 millimetre, with combat sets and a squad RRL 107 millimetres and one rocket set -- combat set of rockets to Mostar." Have you seen the order, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document of the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: You've had a look at it, have you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it in front of me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now let's move on to the next document, which is 3D 01008, also dated the 9th of May, 1993. Once again an order from Brigadier Lasic. It says, "In view of the situation in Mostar I hereby order that a crew for a T-34 tank be sent out and that that same crew should report to the tank battalion in Rodoc at Heliodrom." Can you see the document, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And the next document of the 9th of May once again, 3D 01009 is the number. Another order to the 4th HVO Brigade in Ljubuski to send a PZO 14.5-millimetre piece with crew and 3.000 rounds of ammunition along the Ljubuski-Citluk-Vukodol village axis or route. Do you see the document?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: And just one more document of the of 9th of May. It is 3D 01010. 3D 01010. "In view of the situation in Mostar, I hereby order that the Grdani platoon be sent to Mostar immediately, report to ... " et cetera, et cetera. So this is the last document up to the 9th of May and my question to you is as follows: Would it be normal that somebody intending to prepare an action of attack to write this kind of document two or three days before the 9th of May? Not on that very day, the 9th of May when the attack allegedly took place. So, Colonel, can it be clearly seen on the basis of these documents that somebody was attacked and is facing a difficult situation, and that is seeking urgent assistance in manpower from the surrounding brigades, tank crews, PZO weapons and so on? As a soldier, would you be able to conclude that this man had prepared an action and then on the 9th of May ask that this ordnance be sent out? Now, if you don't wish to answer, that's fine, but let's take a look at the documents.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the number of these individual orders, I as a soldier would conclude that these were reactions, spontaneous reactions to face a certain situation and to rectify it. This was not a pre-planned action. This is how I would assess those orders.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let's take a look at document 3D 01023 next, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, General Praljak showed several documents to the witness. These are documents asking for reinforcement in manpower, in equipment and weapons, ammunition, but we have to see that each document bears a number. 01-2902-93. Then we have one bearing the number 2903-93, then 2909-93. A further one is 2910-93. All these documents seem to be sequential, in order, but there's no 2908, 2907, 2906, 2905, or 2904. It may be that the Defence have those documents. I just wanted to point it out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. There were a lot of documents.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Just take a look at two more document, 3D 01023 is the first one I'd like us to look at. Also dated the 9th of May. It's an important document of the 9th of May, 3D 01023. Once again it says, "In view of the situation in Mostar, I hereby order that six ambulance teams with vehicles be sent to Mostar immediately. Immediately send six ambulance teams," et cetera, "and after arriving to Mostar report to," et cetera. Now, when an offensive action is planned, Colonel, is it the most important thing, as far as the operative elaboration of the plan of attack is concerned, is that the ambulance system and medical system must be -- must go into operation because it is to be expected that there will be a lot of wounded soldiers? So in preparing an attack, the ambulance teams would have to be in Mostar, whereas on the 9th of May this man is asking that six ambulance teams be sent out immediately, and he's in a panic. So would you agree with me that if an action is planned the ambulance teams must be deployed in set locations to be ready and waiting to pull out the wounded?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from a military point of view, the ambulances should follow the troops very closely previously, and in particular, in view of this very narrow area, this would be true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, these questions about what would have been done or the simultaneous orders that were issued, is it possible to judge this if you have no document or no idea of the previous planning? Isn't it also just as possible that ambulances were there already and that for some reason or other, because there was more resistance or resistance was expected, but there could have been other possible reasons for this, or do you think that this was the only possible explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To bring up six ambulances I think is a large number. To assess this more thoroughly about these -- beyond these individual orders, I would have to know the orders of the other side, and you would have to possibly have been actually on site, which means that you would need a very intensive military observation. But the picture given by these six orders gives me a picture of spontaneous reaction, not planning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the transcript, I would like to point out that the last document regarding the ambulances 3D 01023 deals with document 2907, which I mentioned earlier on as missing in the chronology of documents that had been submitted, and this document is -- has now been shown. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... Allowed to say one thing in response to Judge Trechsel's question, just to complete the picture. The burden of proof is on the Prosecution. So far, we have not seen any preparations, any orders of attack for [indiscernible]. So if the document exists, it is up to the Prosecution to produce it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry [Microphone not activated] I have to react to this observation because it seems to imply that I disregard the presumption of innocence. That is a misunderstanding. I have only asked the questions I have asked of the witness because I think it is important to know whether his answer and his reaction to the documents shown can be reliable without the knowledge of all other data that surround it on one side and the other side, and this is not implying in any way that the Defence has the burden to prove anything. I want to clear this. That was a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It -- I had absolutely no intention of saying that, but I just wanted to caution you about that. And the Presiding Judge asked the witness about this a moment ago. The main document which every reasonable soldier must think exists is up to the Prosecution to show. The Defence provides what it has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, very quickly before the break, Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Witness, would you take a look at just one more document before the break. 3D 01021.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to skip over a whole series of documents which follow on the 10th, 11th and 12th of May where he is issuing these orders requesting things in a great panic. And the date of this document is the 10th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It is Miljenko Lasic, although somebody else signed for him, his deputy Petar Zelenika, wrote to UNPROFOR in Zagreb as -- by way of public information, because already on the 10th of May there were speculations made that the HVO was attacking even when it was in a counter-offensive and defending itself and it says, "We are surprised by the statement of the UNPROFOR command concerning the area of the former Yugoslavia that was absolutely supported by no arguments whatsoever, referring to the fact that the HVO forces on the 9th of May started the combat actions in Mostar first, having violated," et cetera, et cetera. "We are amazed that Mr. Wahlgren wasn't objectively informed about the fact who actually did not respect the above-cited agreement and who in fact after numerous provocations started the combat actions on the 9th of May on the barracks of Tihomir Misic." Now, this Tihomir Misic barracks and North Camp which was taken control of later on by the BH army, do you know at the time, that is to say on the 9th of May, it was attacked by the BH army? Did you receive information from any side to that effect?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I knew was what I experienced after I came back on the 25th of July. It was -- there were gaps. The entire picture was so complex that it was difficult to have an overall picture, but I don't know of this letter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, you were down there until the 6th of May. Did you know that the BH army had a completely clear -- clearly elaborated plans to attack the HVO in Mostar? Did you have even the smallest information about their intentions to attack along those lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would inquire whether General Praljak has specific evidence about this or whether this is speculation or conjecture that he's putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know -- you, sir, I don't know if you were here at the time, but precise plans and orders -- well, we showed them here several times with an elaborated map showing the axes of attack, how they wished to attack West Mostar. Those plans were provided on the 19th of April and they're already exhibited here. So they're covered in Arif Pasalic's orders and Mr. Hujka's orders, and the maps and how those maps and plans should be acted upon. And Mr. Pellnas, General Pellnas testified about that here in this courtroom. But I think we're going take the break now and I'll go on with my questions afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have a break. It's now quarter to. We'll resume at five past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Praljak, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kruger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before the break we were still dealing with the question of whether the ABiH had indeed issued specific instructions or was there evidence of planning. I would not like to belabour this point, but I would certainly just wish to make the point in response to General Praljak's response to this that the Prosecution is not entirely sure that it's accurate to say that there is indeed evidence of such planning or plans before the Court. Documents may have been shown to witnesses, but as with this witness, documents are being shown and witnesses are simply being requested to respond, "Have you seen this and is this what the document says." But I think, perhaps, if General Praljak wishes to put this question, certainly it cannot be put in categoric terms, that it is should be if this is put to you, do you have knowledge? Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will decide on the basis of all the evidence adduced by the parties. Please proceed, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, how much time do I have given the fact that I was given 10 minutes by Ms. Nozica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In total you had one hour and 45 minutes. I don't know exactly how much time you've used until now. Certainly one hour. But the registrar will see how much time you've used. Please proceed. I'll tell you later on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the benefit of the OTP, I'll be using two documents, P 02000, P 02000. It's a BH army document dated the 20th of April 1993. The other document is P 1978, dated the 19th of April. This is an order by the 1st Mostar Brigade. These documents have been used before in a very clear manner. This was at a time when Colonel was there with Mr. Pellnas. At the same time, the BH army drafted these orders as they are. The Chamber has these already because they have been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please look at 3D 00916. 3D 00916. This is the foundation: You were at Bijeli Brijeg near the hospital, weren't you? You know the place, and you were there for that meeting. Perhaps you went back at some point to that hilltop location in order to --

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the document yet. Now I have a photograph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... My binder. It's a photograph, yes. These are all photographs. I'll be using a number of photographs now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the benefit of the Chamber, the photographs were taken on the 9th of May, 2007, some two months ago.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: The SpaBat witness claimed that during the clashes on the 9th of May two APCs had been at the plateau near the new hospital in Mostar. Are you familiar with that area? Did you ever go up to that plateau? That's in West Mostar. It's the large hospital where the meeting was held which you attended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a moment. The picture we currently have on screen with number 168 is not in the binder, because in the binder we have a picture numbered 174. So the picture -- the photograph we have on screen at the moment is not in our binder.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is not a photograph. This is a video of what exactly can be seen from that location. The surrounding landscape, if you like. The photographs are just part of the whole thing. In this photograph you can see the new hospital in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, Colonel, do you remember this building, the new hospital building that you can see in this photograph and the surrounding plateau?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the building.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Right. These photographs were taken in segments, one by one, and then moving in a clockwise direction, or perhaps anti-clockwise. So let's go through all these photographs one at a time, please. Sir, as you're looking at these photographs, can you tell me if what we can see here is the same thing that one can see while standing outside the hospital itself? Is this the city of Mostar as seen from in front of the hospital? The document numbers are the same, and the photographs have been placed in a sequence. 178, 179, 180, 181. Have you looked at these, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could imagine that the hospital on the west side is slightly higher, that the photographs have been taken from this place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: These were taken from the flat area in front of the hospital, not from the roof-top of the hospital. There was an APC there. Can we agree with this: Once you reached the flat area outside the hospital and you take a photograph of Mostar you get exactly what we can see in these photographs. Is that consistent with your experience when you were up there, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This goes along with my memory because I was the last time in Mostar in 1995, 1996.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Colonel, we shall now see a video clip. You will see it on the screen. Can the video be played, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: We'll look at the panorama from that same spot. There's a car that can be seen. Let's move on, please. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: To the right you can see the hill of Hum; do you agree, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't have that translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Never mind. Never mind, sir. Never mind, really. It's just the lads taking the footage talking about something. Can you agree with me that this footage was taken from that flat area just outside the new hospital, just as the photographs were, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a German translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: No German interpretation then.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I hear the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. My question again. You see the flat area. Colonel, can you tell us this based on your experience: That video clip and the photographs were taken from the flat area outside the hospital. Is that your impression as well, sir, that that is where they were taken from?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say precisely, but the sweep from left to right corresponds to the image I have in my mind.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Thank you for using a film terminology. I'm referring to your German use of the word "schwenk". Thank you. At this location, at least according to evidence from SpaBat witnesses, there were two APCs when the clashes erupted, what everybody called the HVO attack in Mostar. I asked the previous witness, and I'm asking you now. Considering this location outside these buildings, the buildings that are there, can you see who is standing along the Bulevar, along the confrontation line that had been in place even prior to the 9th of May? Looking from there can you see who is attacking whom? More specifically, let's picture a man standing in that location. Is it possible for that man to see any infantry combat in the centre of town itself along the Bulevar and distinguish clearly who is attacking whom?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the video I think I recognise the building where the 4th armija had it's firing post starting at the left. Details about this I think you cannot see. You can't see what was going on in the street. You can hear noise of fighting. You can hear impacts. You can see smoke and hear fire, but you can't see the troops on the ground from there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you. That is precisely what I was trying to say. I promised the Chamber that I would provide an exact image of this location in order to show what can or cannot be seen from there. Colonel -- rather, if I could ask the Chamber to get an IC number for the map I was tendering a while ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, there was this small map, and we did not assign an IC number to it. Can you please give us an IC number for that map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The small hard-copy map will be IC 613.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As for the time you have left, before we resumed you had 41 minutes left, and you've already used up 15 minutes. So in total you have 26 to 27 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, can you please look at the map that you have to your right. It's on the board. When you arrived there, were you familiar with the disposition of the 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades facing the Serbs or indeed how the BH army troops were positioned in terms of facing the army of the Republika Srpska, or indeed the confrontation line through Mostar down Santiceva Street and the Bulevar? Are you familiar with the forces being deployed in Mostar in precisely this way, and was that the situation when you arrived? There was an HVO brigade to the north of Mostar and another one to the south, as well in as in Mostar itself, near Podvelezje. There was some units there too. The 1st Mostar of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Were you familiar with the deployment of forces in the area, sir, and exactly where they were positioned?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I started, I knew nothing at all about it, but gradually a picture emerged, but I must admit it was very complex. It was very difficult to understand the situation and to form a judgement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: All right. Colonel, sir, I have a purely technical, professional matter to raise with you, a military matter, if you like. I'm not sure if I'll be allowed to ask the question, though. Look at the map, sir, please. What you see on the map is this: If the HVO plans an attack on Mostar - please have a look - would the attack be like this: The 2nd and 3rd HVO Brigades are to the north and south of Mostar respectively, and the forces to the west which are in Mostar itself, can we roughly plan an operation on Mostar like that? Someone planning an attack on Mostar, would they therefore be using the two brigades to the north and south of Mostar respectively in order to attack the BH army forces? Globally speaking, would you raise any objections to that, sir, in your capacity as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, this question is one which goes beyond my competence. I can only say what I have to in all care. I would have to think of it very, very carefully before I gave you an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, I fully understand. I've drawn a different map to show how following that logic the attack would be staged, regardless of the fact that you are refusing to give a clear answer. Nevertheless, can we still display the other map for the benefit of the Colonel where this plan is shown in a more elaborate fashion. But I fully understand your reaction, sir. My question was: With a bare minimum of military logic, would you attack the BH Army from the south, from the north, the North Camp specifically, in the Marsal Tito bridge area? Would you have a sufficient number of ambulances ready to use; your logistics; the stand-by unit; at least a handful of times in the town itself to crush any points of resistance? What would the most elementary military logic, even that which an NCO would be in possession of imply?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect I think it's impossible for the witness to answer this question with the limited amount of information. I think the witness has already said that he cannot answer this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But the question was not put to Mr. Kruger. The question was put to the witness. Colonel, can you answer the question or can't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I refer to historical military examples, I could say you could besiege the place and starve the inhabitants, but basically you would not attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, on these questions what is not to be understood what is the target or what is the objective of the attack? There will be several possibilities, to conquer an entire town or to change the front line. And depending on what the target was, perhaps you could provide a different answer to that very question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said before, Your Honour, I feel that this question is one that I'm unable to answer, and so I am couching my answer in very general terms. Fighting around towns and cities lead to a great deal of victims, and we have examples from the Second World War where we had periods of long siege, but I can't say any more than that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, I thank you for this answer. It is, of course, an exceptionally complex issue. I just wanted to raise some fundamental concerns for this reason simply: There was a full-blown propaganda war going on down there. As of the 9th of May and then for years afterwards it was a universally recognised fact that the attack had been launched by the HVO. I'm just trying to show that this is simply not true. Can we now please play the sniper -- the sniping video. Everybody is talking about the snipers in Mostar. I would like to ask you a number of questions about that, sir. Did you go to the hospital in the west of Mostar? Did you speak to doctors there? Did you ask them how many wounded they were admitting on a daily basis, wounded by bullets, by sniper bullets? I'm talking about civilian casualties. It's difficult to distinguish wounds, of course, but did you at any point get information about how many civilians were being admitted on a daily basis, both Croats and Muslims, who had sustained bullet wounds?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this sort of information was only given to me by way of exception, one of which was the 30th of June where we went to the hospital and talked to -- to the medical officer in charge, and he said he had had five patients, but we -- in general, we didn't have some sort of picture of the number of casualties.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, have a look at the video, please. Let's play it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 3D -- just a minute, please. This footage was taken in West Mostar. [Videotape played].

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the video shows everyone walking around in military uniform as they pleased, ladies and gents alike. Everybody is wearing some sort of uniform or at least parts of a uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 3D 01050. Your Honours, you do have a transcript accompanying this video in your folder, but we can't hear the sound for some reason that I am unaware of.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine. We can stop the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Colonel, my question is this: You were, after all, in an area where there was firing. In Mostar, there are a lot of residential buildings, and the area is densely populated. If you're among those buildings and you're trying to track down the exact location of a sniper, would the sound of a resounding shot be so powerful that somebody might, for all you know, be firing from a building no more than 20 metres away from you and yet, you are still unable to track down the source of the fire, especially since there was a lot of din and a lot of different sources of fire going on for days? We all know that from crime movies, like American shootouts and that sort of thing. In your experience, would it not be exceedingly difficult to discover the exact location of a sniper in the middle of a town like this where there's a lot of firing going on all the time? Would that not be an exceptionally thankless task because of all the shooting that was going on and because of the echo resounding all over the place all the time? Would it not be virtually impossible to define the position of a single sniper? Would your experience not suggest that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think impacts in the proximity would be heard as a loud bang and you could see where they had impacted. It's very difficult to say where the shot is coming from.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
