utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, sir. Just another piece of footage. 3D 001050. I'll ask you this, you were there after all: Do you know that in June 1993 Travnik fell in a way, the BH army having taken Zenica went on to take Travnik as well? Were you aware of that particular development based on documents that you were receiving at the time and that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: General, again in general terms the time you asked me, May, Mostar I was not there, and Travnik was not my area of operations. What I know about Travnik are the reports that I read now and again, and I travelled through Travnik a few times and I was told a bit about Travnik on site, but anything everything else is something which I either read or is purely speculative.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. I am asking you precisely because of any information you may have received. Therefore, do you remember that in June 1993 Travnik was simply taken by the BH army and that there were refugees that fled Travnik at that time? Could we please have the video played?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, we have a technical glitch. The video won't start. Maybe if we get help from someone. Perhaps Mr. Praljak should continue with something else meanwhile.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can we go to the OTP binder. The document number is P 03298. P 03298. Colonel, you didn't answer my question. Based on reports you might have read, were you aware of the fact that Travnik had been taken by the BH army and that there were refugees, some 15.000 Croats who had no choice but to leave the area, fleeing across Mount Vlasic and heading for Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without having seen the document, I can't remember details, and the reason is that in June of that year we were mainly in the area of Jablanica and Konjic, and we were so occupied with many other operations that any further assessments about what was happening elsewhere was something we could only do to a limited extent.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Could you please go to paragraph 6. "SpaBat sector," paragraph 6. The date is the 8th of July, 1993. Paragraph 6, please, "SpaBat sector."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you scroll on this screen? I have it now. I have the "SpaBat sector."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: SpaBat. All right. General situation, it reads: "Fighting continued on the west side of the Neretva River in Mostar." Which we know. But it goes on to say, "Fighting in Boksevica is a still heavy, Jablanica and Konjic were shelled again." Mount Boksevica, is it not above the Kostajnica. Do you know that, sir? Near Konjic. It's the Konjic area. The village of Kostajnica in the Konjic municipality and just behind is Mount Boksevica, which is quite a large mountain.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the mountain well. It's quite clear in my mind of this terrain.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Fine. We'll be going back to Kostajnica. But if we turn the page, the next page of the same document, under 2(B) "Mostar" and then (B)(2) it says, "There is still fierce fighting going on in the area of Bijelo Polje." You were there at the time, and you gave evidence about that. However, I have a general question for you. Why is it that in each and every report while the BH army are attacking Bijelo Polje or Blagaj it says that fighting is going on? And in nine out of ten cases where the HVO are launching a counter-offensive, it reads the HVO are attacking. How come in the area of Konjic we have fighting going on, and as soon as the HVO try to win back their positions or hold the line there is talk of the HVO launching a counter-offensive or even an offensive? How did this get twisted around? Why do we apply two different yardsticks when dealing with the HVO on the one hand and the BH army on the other?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the -- I can't comment on the UNPROFOR reports. On the ECMM, I can say from the example of the 30th of June where we witnessed events or we heard more than otherwise, we clearly related in our reports that the armija soldiers had mutinied against the HVO. And with this example I'm trying to say that we tried to report everything that we had seen in a neutral way without being partisan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Praljak, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Now we come to see Jablanica, Konjic, and point 3 of that section says according to HVO sources at least 30 soldiers were killed in the fighting at Boksevica over the past three days, (3)(C). And now the next document P 03494. 03494. And point 6, again -- or, rather, point 8. Point 8, please. It's a document dated the 16th of July, 1993. Point 8. It says in the second line: "About 200 displaced Croats arrived in Capljina from Kostajnica." My question is this: Do you know that the HVO -- have you found the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't found it yet. I'm still looking.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: It's a Prosecution document. P 03494. Paragraph 8 is the one I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where it says "UNPAs" at the top? Is that the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Figure 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's actually paragraph 6, "SpaBat sector," and under that there are a few paragraphs numbered 1 to 8, and it's paragraph 8 of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It starts with "The villages on each bank." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: That's right. And it says, "About 200 displaced Croats arrived in Capljina from Kostajnica yesterday." Now, my question is this: Do you know that the HVO at Boksevica fought and had over 30 soldiers killed in order to enable civilians from Kostajnica who were -- who threatened to be killed, to pull them out from Boksevica and bring them to Capljina, and there were several hundred of them? Do you know about that, that around the 12th of July Konjic was empty and Kostajnica -- the civilians of Kostajnica were pulled out after defending this axis and that they were brought to Capljina?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before I answer, could I ask whether Capljina is in the direction of Prozor, that is to the west and not to the south? Because I don't know this place.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In the direction of Prozor is west, westward. Kostajnica, and then above Kostajnica you have Boksevica. So do you know that the fighting at Boksevica was very heavy fighting resulting in over 30 persons dead, and then from Kostajnica the civilian population was pulled out and, as you report, were brought to Capljina on the 16th. Is that something you knew about?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were things that I found out later, because I knew Kostajnica fairly well, and I know that the area around Kostajnica had been evacuated of the HVO and civilians. I know that many people went across the mountains. Obviously some of them went south too. I spoke to some of them who had gone over the mountains. For example, a doctor whom I accompanied. And again, to conclude, I didn't find this out on that particular day. It was a certain time afterwards. And I saw Kostajnica when it was empty. And the destruction there was something I looked at again in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you have three to four minutes left. If your video is ready, we might play it now and you might put your question about it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. That's the last thing that I'd like to do, to show the video.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no volume. Just play the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, but it is 3D 00988, the transcript of that footage. For some reason the video doesn't seem to be working. There's no volume, no sound.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Can you see the column of civilians in the background passing by?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a picture in front of me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have to press the video button.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have the picture.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's play the video again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please fast forward.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: Sir, can you see that this is a Serb officer and that the people from Travnik are escaping across Mount Vlasic, that is say, territory controlled by Republika Srpska? My question to you is this: Do you know that in this evacuation from Travnik that the Red Cross took part as well as UNPROFOR and the UNHCR? Are you aware of that? Do you have any knowledge about that, based on the reports that you received?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to overstep the time allotted to me. I'll probably come back to this at some point when the technical booth can play the video with the sound and all the rest, but this is out of love for Herzegovina, 97 per cent of them being Croatians, or is this just expulsion after what happened in Zenica and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: But thank you, Colonel, for your sincere and correct answer. I would like to have gone go over several more topics with you. Well, if the Judges allow me, I'd like to ask you one more question. The 41st Split Brigade is mentioned somewhere there in one of the documents as being present there. Do you know that all the brigades in Croatia except the guards had three digit numbers for names like the 102nd, et cetera, and that the guard brigades just had single digits, the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, et cetera? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: In Croatia, there was never a brigade which would be term the 41st Brigade. Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I might have IC numbers first of all for the video from the hospital, the panorama of Mostar from Siroki Brijeg, and now for the video and the transcript number 3D 01050, and for the last one, too, linked to Vlasic with the partial transcript, and that number is 500988 -- 3D, I'm sorry, 3D 900 whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please give us some numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The video panorama from the hospital becomes IC 614; the sniper video 3D 01050 becomes 615; and the last video, 3D 00988 becomes IC 616.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I now have the 6D team. They have 45 minutes, and then we'll have 4D with one hour and 15 minutes. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we begin, my colleague and I, Ms. Alaburic and I, want to be practical. We would even be prepared to shorten our time. It depends how much the Prosecution needs for redirect and the Judges' questions, and perhaps we could even conclude today. So can we hear what Mr. Kruger has to say about that first?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Well, at this juncture, Mr. Kruger, what do you think? How much time for the redirect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's very difficult to say. At this stage if we had to redirect now I would have been asking for probably about five minutes, but it of course depends on what happens after this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Nissen, good afternoon. My name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb, and together with my colleague Mr. Nicholas Stewart, I'm Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic. I'd like to start off by trying to clarify some matters to see what actually happened on the 30th of June, 1993. And, if possible, could the witness be given the Prosecution binder, because I'll be using Prosecution documents as well as my own. Let's me remind you, Colonel Nissen, the Prosecutor asked you about the 30th of June, 1993, as being an event characterised by a BH army attack on North Camp. The same description on that day is contained in the indictment. In response to that question, your answer was that from various sources you learnt that individual soldiers of the BH army, and perhaps units, too, of the BH army, but most probably individual soldiers, rose up against the HVO. And now let me put my question right. Not individuals in the BH army, but soldiers, individuals in the HVO. Individual soldiers in the HVO. Do you remember that answer of yours, Colonel Nissen?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the reports we received. These were Muslims, if I may say so, who were serving in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now try and see whether it was only North Camp, and later on we'll try and analyse whether it was Muslim individuals and what the consequences of that event were. Let's start off by looking at a document in my binder. It is P 03031, and it is a document of the European monitors dated the 30th of June, 1993. It is a daily report in the section for Mostar. This is what it says: "The army took control of the HVO north barracks, the dam, and the village of Rastani, which is on the west bank. The attack was not confirmed which was allegedly carried out in a more northerly area towards Bijelo Polje." Now, this is the monitor's report, and it would emerge that on the 30th of June it wasn't only North Camp that was attacked but that the attack was broader in scope. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was much larger and that it also was -- went to the south. We didn't know that at that moment in time, only on the 30th of June. As to how far the area was where the fighting took place in the north, we didn't know about it at that time. It only transpired later on how large the area was.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In view of that answer of yours, I'm going to skip over the next two documents which I had intended to put to you and ask you to take a look at the following document, 4D 00621. It is a diagram in colour similar to the one shown to you by General Praljak earlier on, but this is in a more practical A4 format. I can see that you've found it. Colonel Nissen, the blue designates the HVO, the green is the BH army, the Serbian army comes next, behind the red line to the right and this is the situation as it was before the 30th of June, 1993. To the best of your knowledge, does this correspond to the situation on the ground? Does this map correspond to the situation on the ground and that the BH army was in control of the town of Mostar which we call East Mostar, that the BH army held East Mostar, that the HVO had the 2nd Brigade towards the north, touching along the Serb lines and the 3rd Brigade southwards towards the Serb positions. And after that in the north and south we have areas under BH army control. Is that how it was, Colonel Nissen? They've just told me that in the south it was exclusively the area of Blagaj, because in continuation southwards that was the territory under the control of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This corresponds to roughly the picture that we had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say approximately, perhaps we could clear the point up straight away, or do you say that because you don't have any precise information about that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For example, we didn't know exactly where the line to the Serbs was. It was -- there certainly weren't that many soldiers that there wasn't a proper line as such any more, I imagine. And in the north I got the impression that the line of the HVO, it might be a little bit further south, that -- that were my ideas when I first looked at the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, let's take a look at document 4D 00622 now, please. It shows the situation after the 30th of June, 1993. And we have the axis of attack of the BH army marked here. Under 1 is North Camp then we have Rastani, Vrapcici, Bijelo Polje in order and Potoci, Blagaj and Buna is shown as an intended axis of attack, but the BH army did not manage to gain control of that area. Now, tell us, please, Colonel Nissen, to the best of your knowledge does this diagram correspond to what was happening on the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of June we didn't have any idea about the fact that it was a closed area from Mostar to Blagaj, that that could exist. I assume that this picture was only -- only occurred later on, on the terrain later on. Pointing out our reports that were drawn us -- up later on, I think it was said that the picture slowly emerged of a closed link of the east of the Neretva from the north to the south. This -- so this would roughly correspond to this picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Colonel Nissen, what you're saying is that you didn't have knowledge that that happened on the 30th of June, 1993, but that that was the general tendency and that it was the actual situation several days later. Am I right in thinking that?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That what happened on the 30th of June in Mostar, we interpreted that as we reported. It was like it was an uprising, which at that moment in time we couldn't assess whether the uprising would be successful or whether it would ended by prisoners being taken or there would be further attacks or it would canceled out. We didn't know that at the time. So only with time we got the complete picture. Beforehand, it was a bit deceptive. I'm looking at in practical terms. There is a check-point, then there is a small group that is fighting. In another place, you would have an occupied house. It looks so operational where the things were very simple, but it wasn't like that in my opinion, because very slowly the armija gained influence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Petkovic would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to ask you the following question. This situation in the south, in your opinion, is that what happened until the 13th of July, and do you remember your report of the 13th of July in which you described that? And I refer to a Prosecution document, P 03427.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. Colonel Nissen, I don't think you will find the document in our binder, we haven't prepared it, the document raised by my client just now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in the Prosecution binder, and the witness did refer to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Nissen, would you look in the Prosecution binder then, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've got it in front of me now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: P 03427 is the document number. Let us look at point 3 where it says "Military activity," and the document is dated the 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't get any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's me repeat. Point 3 of that document where it says, "Military activities."

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you state: "There have been army attacks in the area of the Dubrava plateau, which is the region of Stolac, Capljina, and Buna." Having looked at this clip, can you tell where Buna is or where the general axis described here might be, having looked at the sketch?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a line from west to east, south of Mostar. A -- quite a few kilometres south of Mostar. I'm referring to your question Buna-Blagaj. And the other line, it goes roughly from south-east to north-west in a slightly angular direction, if I can say it like that. It would be easier to show it on the map really. But just maybe to put it like this, according to the question, it's a further movement towards south.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. I'm referring to the map you were shown by my attorney south of Mostar. Blagaj and Buna, that's the area I'm talking about. And I put it to you in your document of the 13th of July this is exactly how you describe it. The attack unfolded in the direction of Gubavica and Buna. Gubavica is even further south than Buna, but they didn't take Gubavica.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all I can say about this for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Any clearer now sir? Thank you. Now I would like to invoke another document that you produced. It's about the northern part. This is also an OTP document. This is P 03298. Let us look at paragraph 6 of that document, sir. "SpaBat sector." Please try to find paragraph 6, sir. There is a comment just under it. Have you got it? According -- according to Zuka -- Zuka is a person you're familiar with. According to Zuka, the BH army can walk across the whole eastern bank of Neretva from Jablanica to Mostar. If the army can walk along at that line, does that not mean that the army's now in control of the whole Sector North along the Neretva River? I'm talking in relation to Mostar itself, having as a consequence linked up with the forces at Jablanica. There is reference there to the Colakovac dam, which are now where it is, don't you, sir? Near the Bijela Bridge. You know where Vrdi is, and I think you know where Dreznica is. Isn't that what your document says?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what -- I've got it in front of me. I've got it more or less roughly. I looked at it. I've understood it and I can now answer your questions. I got it now. Maybe you can ask the question again that -- so that I'm -- that would enable me to give a more precise answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PETKOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Back to the sketch that my attorney was using. She can ask the question. Is the sketch that we made consistent with the documents that you produced?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank General Petkovic for his contribution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel, before you go on and answer this question I would like to remind you of one thing, one particular document that we've already looked at in this court, where there is an explicit conclusion, and this is the same conclusion that General Petkovic is drawing your attention to. It's in the OTP binder and the number is 3361. 3361. Paragraph 6 of that document. (6)(C)(3) reads: "It has been confirmed that the BH army forces have succeeded in linking up their units from Mostar with those from the Jablanica area," which is in the north of this map. This is precisely what General Petkovic has drawn here, and this is precisely what his question is in reference to. Can we therefore conclude beyond any doubt that the east part of Mostar was linked up with the BH army units that were north of Mostar just as shown in this sketch?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took me quite a while, because it looked quite operational. I don't want to make any mistakes. But basically the fact that there was a link, that is true. That is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, my question was probably phrased in a way that was somewhat clumsy, but I asked the question as though all of this had happened just after the 30th of June, 1993, which is simply not correct. Part of this happened at that time, and part of this happened over the following two weeks. Therefore, this sketch would be consistent with the situation on the 13th of June, 1993 -- 13th of July, 1993, based on all the reports we have so far seen. Can we agree on that, sir? They're telling me it might be useful to repeat the number. 4D 00622. That is the number for that sketch, just in case you have mislaid it. So now you will be able to find it again. That's right. Can we agree, sir, that this was indeed the situation in mid-July 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 30th of June or a few days later, we understood it to be a picture which was very scattered, but afterwards we understood that it was a cohesive line from the north, with a link to the north. It looked initially like a patchwork, but then it was a cohesive line.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see if this was really a question of individual betrayal among the Muslims in the HVO or perhaps there was a broader, organised action conducted by the Muslims within the HVO. Let's begin by looking at P 03025, which is another ECMM report. The date is the 30th of June. Paragraph 5, please. Section 4. It reads: "This morning between 3.00 and 4.00 the Muslim soldiers, members of the HVO battalion in --"

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the numbers slowly? I don't have the document in front of me. Could you give me the numbers again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Can you look at my binder, please, my set of documents, not the OTP set of documents. It's in my set under your left hand. That's right. P 03025.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the document which goes to Zenica, the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: This is an ECMM document, the one I'm talking about. Look at paragraph 5, please. Section 5 of paragraph 5. Describing the treason of the Muslim soldiers. It says that the Muslim soldiers who were within the HVO battalion Bijelo Polje attacked the Croat troops and positions in that area, specifically the village of Rastani on the west bank and the northern barracks of the HVO. These attacks were coordinated ahead of time and enjoyed the support of the 1st Mostar Brigade, whereas the commander of the 2nd Brigade, Midhat Hujdur was killed in the fighting. There were 20 wounded soldiers in the HVO hospital, as well as three wounded civilians and three bodies belonging to HVO soldiers. Colonel Nissen, can you confirm that this is an authentic report produced by the ECMM, and can you confirm the accuracy of the information contained therein?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The format is slightly different so I really have to look at it more closely. To confirm this precisely, I would have to read it in detail because the format is rather strange, but basically it looks okay, but I really would have to read it. Is this a copy of our report or what?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nissen, what I really want to know right now --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry, if I may assist my colleague here that this is an electronic copy of an ECMM document received electronically, so it does come from the ECMM. That explains for Colonel Nissen why the format would look different. Thank you, Your Honour. It's already admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Then I confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, does it not follow based on this document that this was no treason by Muslim individuals in the tanks of the HVO but, rather, that what was at stake here was an organised activity of a much broader scope, one that was linked to the BH army, since Mr. Midhat Hujdur took part, was involved in these activities and was killed in the process?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The fact that it was a planned or a major action is something which we were clear about afterwards. With the events of this day after we came back to the CC and we were so occupied with the formulation that we couldn't make any conclusions at that point. That would have been premature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, in order not to waste time any more discussing and belabouring this point, that these were not individual actions taken by Muslims in the HVO but, rather, a broader operation? Any information gleaned later on about this only seemed to confirm this theory, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't confirm something that we hadn't known previously, but let me say once more quite clearly at the beginning it seemed to us that it was a spontaneous activity from -- on the part of individual soldiers that could have taken place for different reasons, but by the middle of July we thought that this could have been part of some sort of larger operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since we're still not certain, let's look at another document, an UNPROFOR document. The number is P 097 -- 02979. This is an UNPROFOR document, a weekly report. Can you have a look, please, sir? P 02979. It's in my set of documents, the one that I have provided.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 5, sir. 5(3) -- 5(A)(3). UNPROFOR states Muslims are leaving the 1st and 3rd Brigades of the HVO and are joining units the BH army. Colonel, did you have any information to indicate that Muslims at this stage were leaving the HVO on a massive scale?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in fact this was something that I gleaned from later picture, a more complete picture, not so quickly or during the time period that one could imagine. We had to react with a certain time lag, even in our thoughts so that we could formulate a picture. So these were images which came later, not ad hoc. And this also had to do with the fact our movements were restricted, and because we could not only rely on the reports of other entities like UNPROFOR, for example.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, did you know that these Muslims as they were leaving the HVO took with them weapons, ammunition, medical supplies and such like, whatever they deemed might be helpful once they had joined their new army?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We found this out, too, and we thought that that was the case, in fact, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, did you know that -- this is about the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, and we saw the positions they were holding around Mostar. That in the 2nd Brigade of the HVO the percentage of Muslim soldiers was about 40 per cent?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these percentages were not known to us. We assumed, rather, from the point of view of the time that everything that was around about Mostar had fewer armija soldiers and that in the area left of the Neretva, in this area and the brigade of Obradovic there were considerably more armija soldiers. This is how we saw things at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, I'm not asking you about BH army soldiers. I'm asking you about the HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, of Muslim faith, if you like. I'm telling you that the HVO contained 40 per cent of Muslim soldiers. I'm talking about the 2nd Brigade.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again percentages were unknown to us. I can only give you a more general assessment. The more -- the closer the brigades were to Mostar, the HVO brigades, the fewer armija soldiers were there. And the further they moved to the south - this is why I referred to the brigade of Obradovic - there were more armija soldiers in these brigades. The reason, I would say, was that at a much later point in time I found out that at least parts of complete armija brigade was in the south, something which I hadn't known for a long time. They were in houses and apartments and so on, allegedly. But about the numbers that you're asking, in terms of actual percentages or so I can't answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us leave these figures aside for the time being, Colonel Nissen. Let us try to clarify this: I'm asking you about Muslims in the HVO. Regular HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity. I'm not asking you about the BH army, I'm not asking about any of their brigades. I'm asking you about the regular HVO soldiers who happened to be of Muslim ethnicity, who on the 13th [as interpreted] of June, 1993, rose up against an army which had they had up to that point served? I am asking you about the percentage of Muslims in the HVO. It would be quite sufficient for you to tell me whether you knew about the percentage of Muslims in the 2nd Brigade of the HVO, whether you knew that the percentage was relatively high.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something we found out later. I admit that at the beginning we considered the proportion to be smaller, but we had no doubt about it, and I refer you again to the report of the 30th [Realtime transcript read in error "13th"] of June. We spoke immediately of mutiny, and this means in military terms these are so soldiers of this army who had risen up against the leaders in this army, that is the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Before I move on, two corrections for the transcript. In my question, page 66, line 1, the date is the 30th of June and not the 13th. And the witness's answer, page 66, line 9, the witness was actually talking about the 30th of July and not about the 13th of June as the transcript reflects. All right. Let's continue. Mr. Nissen, you wrote in your reports about the fact that Colonel Obradovic had told you that in his own HVO brigade, which was the 1st Brigade of the HVO, the percentage of Muslims was 25, 25 per cent. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember so precisely because this was a number which I derived from the other team. I -- I could only read about it and talk to them about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. For those who want to check the percentages reflected in P 03175. Colonel Nissen, if indeed this information is correct about the 40 per cent of Muslims in the 2nd Brigade, 25 per cent of Muslims in the 1st Brigade, not to mention the percentage figures as they relate to other brigades, at a time when we have this treason on a massive scale by the Muslims on the one hand and the HVO losing territory precisely because of this on the other, because of this treason, could we then not say that at this point in time the HVO was severely weakened and something had to be done quickly were the HVO to preserve control over the territory that was in their hands at the time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you are saying, apart from these percentages, if so many soldiers rebel, then in this case many HVO soldiers and leaders are occupied in finding out who they are, to guard them and to take them somewhere else, and the troops are almost laid lame for other matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Given the circumstances, the decision was made for the remaining Muslims who were still members of the HVO to be disarmed and detained. Following certain investigative steps, a decision was to be made and proceedings were to be initiated or else they -- they would just be allowed to return to their units. Were you familiar -- were you familiar with that decision made by the HVO authorities at the time?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you of a document that we've been looking at over the last couple of days. This is in the Prosecutor's set. P 03427. 03427. This is a report dated the 13th of July. There's an account here of a conversation with Mr. Kresimir Zubak. Among other things, Kresimir Zubak goes on to explain that it was necessary to detain the Muslim soldiers within the HVO because they had committed treason. They had organised or staged an uprising. Does this jog your memory, sir? Do you perhaps after all remember that the HVO took a decision of this nature? They informed all of their collocutors about this, which included the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now we're again about the middle of July, and such information, although I can't remember precisely what you're asking, but the information as a whole of course had to come together, so we knew also with the -- about the discussion with Mr. Zubak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to break. We'll have a 20-minute break. The Defence told us that they might conclude today. We have 1 hour and 10 minutes left. After the break we'll have 1 hour left. The Defence told us that they wanted to conclude today, so please try to do so if at all possible. We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, for purposes of continuity, let me repeat and recapitulate. We were talking about Mr. Kresimir Zubak who informed the European Monitors about the need to arrest the Muslim soldiers in the HVO. I'd like to ask you the following questions, and ask them to the best of your knowledge, information you learnt then, afterwards and so on. Can we agree that after the BH army in April 1993 took certain offensive action vis-a-vis the HVO that absolutely nothing bad happened to the Muslim soldiers within the HVO. That is to say, none of them were disarmed, arrested, or anything else adverse in that sense?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have now mentioned the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Konjic.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I have would see this month rather in terms of the north, in Klis, in terms of the attacks the armija, not particularly in the area of Mostar. I wouldn't bring the two together.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, I didn't intend to link it up to the events in Mostar. What I wanted to do was to look at the broader area, the area that you were in charge of, and tie up some facts there, and so I wanted to see if you agreed with my assessment to the effect that after the BH army offensive in April 1993 on the territory of Konjic nothing bad happened to the Muslims who were soldiers in the HVO. They continued to fight alongside their fellow combatants, Croats, within the HVO units; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I could confirm that. In spite of the attacks of the armija in the north, there were no changes within the units in the south.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, can we also agree with the following statement, that not even in June 1993 when the BH army took control of the area of Travnik, Kakanj, and Fojnica can anything bad happen to the Muslim soldiers in the HVO, that none of them were disarmed, taken into custody, or degraded in any way whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I and obviously others, other observers, saw nothing about this. I'm talking about the UNPROFOR people. There were no such reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving the interpretation. Ah, yes, I am now. Thank you. Yes, reports of that kind or, rather, observations of that kind are not contained in any of the monitor reports. Now, would you agree with me when I say the following, and I think we've already agreed mostly, it was only on the 30th of June, 1993, when the mass treachery of the Muslims within the HVO ranks occurred, the HVO decided for security reasons to disarm and arrest the Muslims in the HVO? Would that be right? And you reported on that event, you and other monitors. Do we agree on that point?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like us now to take a look at a Prosecution document in the Prosecution binder. The number is P 0347. We've already looked at it today. Maybe you don't even have to look for the document. I have a simple question. It is a report from the ECMM for the 15th of July, 1993, and in a part of that report it says that group M3 informed that all the Muslim soldiers, 400 of them -- between 4 and 500 of them in Tomislavgrad were disarmed and sent home. Mr. Nissen, do you remember that part of the report? And in that regard, I'd like to ask you the following question, it's about Tomislavgrad: Now, Tomislavgrad, was it a town in Herzegovina with an absolute majority population?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have said, and it is so in the transcript on line 15, P 0347. Are you not referring to 30427?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document number is 3470. Yes, 0 at the end. It's a document that we've already looked at, and we've already heard that piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'd just like us to analyse this, how come that something like that happened in Tomislavgrad. So my question refers to Tomislavgrad. Do you know that it's a town in Herzegovina where the majority population is Croatian and a town that was never any part of BH army offensives? Can we agree on that point?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although surrounding areas around Tomislavgrad certainly had had a Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you also agree with me when I say that precisely for the reason I mentioned earlier on there were no security reasons for the Muslim soldiers to be disarmed or arrested and that that is why they were sent home, as was recorded in this ECMM report?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We saw that Mr. Kresimir Zubak had informed the European Monitors of the necessity to arrest Muslim soldiers in the HVO. Now, tell me, please, Colonel Nissen, did you know that other institutions were informed of that as well, for example, the UNHCR, the International Red Cross committee being two cases in point?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, whether we informed them directly I can't say, but the reporting system, as such, required an exchange of documents amongst ourselves. So from the normal source of procedures, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. We've already seen the document in court. It is a Prosecution document in his binder. P 3554 is the number. And in that document it says that the UNHCR was informed of the Muslims taken into custody and that the HVO asked their assistance in moving the Muslim detainees and refugees. Now, from these documents -- well, Colonel, if you wish to take a look you can. It is under point 4 relating to the humanitarian situation in the document that I've just read out. On the basis of all these documents and on the basis of your own personal knowledge, can we agree that the HVO, without wasting time, asked the assistance of the UNHCR and other international institutions in order to take care of the Muslims that had been taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least according to this report the UNHCR had been sufficiently informed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: According to the documents and the witnesses who testified in this courtroom, there's no doubt that the UNHCR refused to help the HVO and explained this by saying that their assistance would be a contribution to the so-called ethnic cleansing. I say so-called or alleged ethnic cleansing because it's not a concept that has been defined by any legal regulations. It is a concept used by journalists, which has come into frequent use. Now, do you have any knowledge about that, that is to say that the UNHCR, with the explanations that they provided, refused to help in solving the problem of the Muslims who had been arrested? And I think that's what it says in the document that we looked at a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a particularly difficult situation. We talked about this in a similar form yesterday. At the moment when the HVO was burdened with those prisoners that we were talking about yesterday, or unburdened, rather, they're free for fighting, and the UNHCR felt that they had a certain responsibility, and it removed the burden from the HVO at least to concern themselves with these prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But the UNHCR did not help the HVO, so that all these Muslims in detention were left with the HVO to deal with them alone; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to say that that was absolutely true is something I can't confirm, because I really don't know. But I think the principle is okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, to the best of your knowledge the HVO never prepared itself for a situation in which they would have so many Muslims arrested or anybody else, for that matter. You didn't report on this, that the HVO was building detention centres or getting ready for any mass arrests. You agree with me there, don't you? There were no preparations for any mass arrests and Muslim detentions on the part of the HVO, nor did you ever notice anything of that kind? And I'm referring to the situation up to the 1st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no knowledge of anything like this taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm going to offer you a conclusion. If it's just speculation tell me so, but I put it to you that if there were no activities towards opening any detention centres or any preparations for mass arrests, and if the arrests on the 1st of July were a consequence of treachery on the part of the Muslim soldiers within the HVO ranks, would it be well-founded to conclude that there was no plan on the part of the HVO to imprison Muslims on the territory of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only refer to what we discussed before. The HVO presumably assumed that the Muslim soldiers would be safe because they had fought on their sides, and the situation was the reverse in the north. There were -- the HVO soldiers were fighting the armija, and they saw the need to take particular measures, I can't judge, but to make such preparations. I'm referring to these soldiers once more that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let me be practical. Now, if on the 30th of June we have the treachery of the Muslims, and if on the 1st of July the HVO makes a decision to disarm and arrest the Muslims within the HVO, then it would be well founded to conclude that there was no criminal plan of arresting Muslims among HVO ranks. Do you agree with me, based on what you know?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that this plan did not exist according to the events, because if they had had such a plan, then they could have intervened at an earlier stage to save lives. So this would have been the logical consequence, and then there would have been fewer casualties and fewer deaths. When I think of a family that I interviewed, refugees, from the area of Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel Nissen. I'd now like to ask you, and my time is running out, to explain something that you said. It was in response to a question asked by my colleague Ms. Senka Nozica. Let me remind you. You told us, and in a statement to the Prosecutor in 1998 you said that at the end of April 1993 you gained the impression that the Muslims were trying to expel the Croats from the southern part of Central Bosnia, and my colleague Senka Nozica asked you about that. Now, in continuation you went on to say, "Later on I understood that that was a concept. That was the conception." What did you have in mind, this concept of the BH army in taking control of areas which until then had been under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the month of April many more meetings took place on all military levels than had been clear before on all levels, and then we had individual sorties or visits to Jablanica, Konjic, and the area north of the Jablanica lake. These were individual activities, and at that time, this is why I talk about joint commissions, General Petkovic, Pasalic, and Lasic, and the entire staff, they were still working. There was a whole series of other people, Ramic and other peoples, who were all cooperating. So that everything took place in April. And then these attacks increased so that looking back, and I'm being very careful here, one could say that it was almost a manoeuvre to deceive each other. I think one should take this, however, very carefully. But afterwards, looking back everything that was done was fairly useless. All the commissions and attempts to create a cease-fire wouldn't have been needed, but there were signs. And this brings me back to Zuka and to the brigade commander of the armija. There were signs, and there were considerable forces opposing the high-ranking military people, and they wanted something different, and I think, as I said before, Mr. Zuka attacked Halilovic openly, quite energetically, and said that he would cooperate with the Croats and the Serbs and that he was not going to go along with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Colonel Nissen, for the very end I'd like you to take a look at a document in my binder. It is P 02740. It is a report by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And may we go into private session, because it is a document under seal. I apologise for not mentioning that straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, and I'm giving the floor to Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As we were saying, Colonel, you know the person I mean. He was a colleague of yours working in the ECMM during that period of time; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He deputised for me during my leave in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It was from the 6th of May to the 25th of May, 1993, was it not? And you appointed him your deputy, did you not? What kind of cooperation did you have with the gentleman, Mr. Milverton?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely how long he was in Mostar, but he went to another post and he was no longer my deputy. But I think I can say on this occasion I'd like to ask the Prosecutor or point out if I may, Your Honour, that with regard to ECM monitors from the Foreign Office of the Federal Republic of Germany, I can only limit my statements. My statements are restricted on that count.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber has taken due note of what you said. Please proceed, Mr. Ibrisimovic, taking into account what the witness has just said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness during his evidence has mentioned his name so many times that he stood in for him in Mostar throughout this period of time. I'll try to ask the witness this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Milverton on your return to Mostar on the 24th, possibly the 25th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I had more to do with the Dutch monitors, personally, but I can't really confirm that. It would have been a matter of course for my deputy to be there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The natural thing would be upon your return for your deputy to brief you, to submit a report to you of some kind, wouldn't it? Hence my question. Did you talk to him when you returned to Mostar?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you can remember, did you hold a meeting with him upon your return?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a meeting in Mostar west, and looking at this Croatian document Peter Espensen is mentioned here. He was an UNPROFOR or UNMO officer who led the meeting. He was there too obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir. Please don't look at the document before I start pointing things out to you. First try to answer my questions and then we'll go back to the document.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took part in a meeting where Espensen chaired the meeting, the UNMO officer, and Nigel Milverton was present.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Is this the same meeting that you spoke of in terms of representatives of the civilian authorities being there on the 25th of May, 1993? It was about electricity, about water. Water and electricity supplies and such like.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is the meeting that I'm talking about, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you have a look at the document in front of you now. For the benefit of the transcript this is P 02512. Attending the meeting was Mr. Milverton, as well as Mr. Espensen. I don't see your name there, though, so what I want to know is was this the same meeting that you attended or are we talking about a different meeting?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came into this meeting quite spontaneously because I had just come back, but it must have been the same meeting. Without looking at the document I'm saying this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You can have a look, sir. It's not a long document. Take your time, please. You see the preamble; right? You talked about the agreement dated the 12th of May, 1993, between General Halilovic and General Petkovic, General Morillon and Ambassador Thebault. The agreement was reached by the negotiating parties there was someone on behalf of the HVO and someone on behalf of the BH army. This is a logical conclusion or continuation, if you like, of that agreement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The agreement was witnessed by the international community, wasn't it? Your own associate, Mr. Milverton, as well as military observer Espensen. You said it yourself, after all, that you chanced on that meeting as it were, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 1, paragraph 2, and paragraph 3, you see that persons were appointed to implement this agreement. The signatories, needless to say, are responsible for seeing the agreement through, seeing it implemented. The agreement was additionally authorised and endorsed, if you like, by the international community. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as they have signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you go to paragraph 7 -- yes, of course. Paragraph 7. This is precisely what you talked about when you saw those buses; right?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going back to a particular portion of your evidence. You said, "We heard there was something going on. We heard rumours, so I was out there myself." Therefore, you were present, one of your associates, fellow monitors, was present, and this was more than just rumours. This was something that you were deeply involved in, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to reconstruct how this day went on. It -- things were very confused, and Nigel Milverton had prepared this matter, and he was the ECMM participant in the meeting responsible and he signed. And I was with the Dutch monitor out in the town, looking around the town and the vicinity. We were together in one car. And we didn't grasp everything that went on in the meeting, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, this would seem to be an exceptionally important meeting, wouldn't it? It was expected that Mr. Milverton would be briefing you on the substance of the meeting. The International Red Cross were involved. UNPROFOR were too. That is why I'm saying these were no mere rumours. This was an agreement that was being implemented based on what was eventually signed, and one of your associates was there.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the fact that it was a signed document like the one I see in front of me now, this was something that at that time when my report was made on the observations of the bus transports was something that I didn't know, and this does not change the situation that I described when talking about the bus transports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you look at this document, you see that Mr. Pusic received no assignment whatsoever to be part of this agreement, to be part of its implementation. Can we please go to the other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think these documents are under seal, and I think it might be best for us to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You saw the agreement, sir.

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this question: If on the 25th of May at this meeting where the agreement was signed, one of your associates from the monitor mission attended. Furthermore, there was a military observer involved in it, the International Red Cross, SpaBat. This was an open secret, wasn't it? Why did you feel that your presence on the spot was undesirable since you all knew about this going on and you were, in fact, all deeply in it, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the situation in front of buses, because we had been told that we have nothing to do with this matter and we should go away. And let me add that I don't know this document, and I'm extremely surprised that General Pasalic has signed this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Your associate from the monitoring mission, too, thereby in some way endorsing it. It wasn't just General Pasalic, was it?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Obviously he had signed it, too, yes. To say quite clearly, and I'm repeating what I said in terms of my restricted statements, this is something that he should have presented to me, or he should have reported this more accurately than perhaps the assessment that I had in the evening with the other monitor could have turned out quite different. Not in terms of what we saw but possibly in the assessment of the situation. What we saw, we saw. It's also possible that the affected population, I'm only saying this with hindsight now, that the population affected would have reacted in a different way had they been dealt with in a different way, different according to the plans of what had been going on in their community.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. President, this is sufficient for our purposes. No more questions for us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kruger, do you have any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I confirm that Ms. Tomic and the Coric Defence have no questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, just two matters that I would like to raise briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Colonel, this afternoon General Praljak showed you a selection of about six or seven documents from the 9th of May, 1993, on the basis of which you stated that, "Based on these documents it seems to me this could be a spontaneous reaction." My question to you, Colonel, is if you had more documents at your disposal pre-dating the 9th of May, would this in any way -- or could this in any way affect this assessment of yours that this is a spontaneous reaction?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say that it would require a much wider assessment of both sides to make a final judgement. I don't know whether individual documents would be helpful in this respect. I fear they wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. The other matter that I would like to briefly touch upon is last night Mr. Karnavas, he read two very dramatic documents, and this morning you also raised these same documents when we started the session. Now, sir, the response that you gave yesterday to these documents was, in essence, that you did not personally know about the events or the matters raised in those documents or described therein, and also that these related to events outside your area of responsibility. My question, the first one, is what, as an ECMM monitor, was your responsibility, if any, regarding events which occurred outside your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I read that as a report, and this would be the normal situation, I had no responsibility because I would assume, according to the reporting system, that all of those with responsibility in this matter would have taken the responsibility. We would not normally have telephoned a comrade in another office, in other institution, to say, "Look, something has happened over there." This is not part of the normal working situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: And, sir, would you necessarily have known what the precise steps were which would have been taken in somebody else's area of responsibility with regard to all matters that occurred there?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't necessarily have found out, but perhaps with a certain time delay, and I may have noted some report in the press or other publications, but I wouldn't have received this on the normal -- during the normal reporting system. I might have received a summary after a certain amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you raised those two -- or the issues or those two documents this morning. Was there anything further you wished to add with regard thereto?

utterances.speaker: KLAUS JOHANN NISSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say that if I have received original documents, I was very careful to assess whether they were forged or real. It's very difficult when you're working on site. These documents, I had no reason to doubt their authenticity, are hopefully being submitted to all sorts of forensic investigations, but I was very careful with the documents as far as their originality was concerned and also in terms of the signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRUGER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just for the sake of general information, Mr. Kruger began with those six or seven documents that Mr. Praljak had previously shown the witness, dated the 9th of May, all issued by the same commander, Commander Lasic. I suppose you noticed during the examination that the numbers -- document numbers are in a series, which in some way shows their authenticity but some numbers are missing. I've checked with my office since, and I can't quite say we have all of those, but I believe we are actually in the possession of nine out of ten. Maybe even all of them. I can't promise that, but we have all or nearly all of those documents that's as far as the missing numbers are concerned. I also received an e-mail from one of my associates, we weren't planning on using those, simply because they had not yet all been translated. We picked a couple of typical documents that Mr. Praljak used. As for the other documents, we can forward this sort of information to you later on, the numbers and whatever else. If there's time, if there is a need, I'll be showing them to you. Even if we had them in our hands, certainly we wouldn't be using all of them because time was short. Perhaps we can simply serve you notice of the document numbers and perhaps submit photocopies, not as evidence but merely to prove that we have the entire series of documents in our possession. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... for these explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I wonder if I might have a moment. Yesterday, at the conclusion of the session, the gentleman witness, who has been very patient and very proper, was rather agitated having believed that perhaps I was suggesting that he had come across these orders, and that as a military man and as an observer had done nothing. And I indicated to him that I would clarify the matter. I didn't want to speak to him because obviously he's a witness, and I understand this was raised earlier on and was raised by my colleague Suzana Tomanovic, but just to make sure that the gentleman understands. First, I want to apologise if I offended him, that wasn't the intention. Two, I never suggested nor am I suggesting that those orders were shown to the document -- to the gentleman or were available to him because obviously what the orders call for were something rather horrendous and something that one would keep in confidence assuming that they had intentions of putting that to plan, which is our -- our belief that that was the case. So -- and the purpose for showing the documents was again to demonstrate that there were things happening that were, one, unavailable, or unknown to the ECMM monitors but secondly there was a document that was shown by Mr. Kruger to the gentleman where in the document itself the commander of the army of BiH indicated to the ICRC, this is from -- to BritBat, that he was no longer going to take prisoners, meaning that he would give no quarter and that he would be executing prisoners. So I used that as an opportunity to introduce those documents. Again, I want to make sure that the gentleman understands that there was no insinuation that he himself was aware of those documents or those events and he did not act, and there was no insinuation that he did not act properly while he was there as an observer. I want to make sure that the gentleman understands and again, to the extent that I may have caused you any pain, I apologise. That was not my intention. Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well, Colonel, your testimony has come to an end, unless Mr. Praljak wanted to apologise as well. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no reason for me to do that. Your Honour, you said before the witness began about those 95 binders containing 100 documents, roughly speaking, the ones that I mentioned. There are over 8.000 documents contained therein. That's one thing. In answer to Mr. Kruger, documents were tendered that pre-date the 9th of May. I did show a number of documents to show exactly what the area commander was reporting prior to the 9th of May. I did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, since probably we won't be in session tomorrow, and I should say good evening, Your Honours, Mr. President and the other Judges. If I could just raise one procedural matter. The Defence, various Defence teams have filed various responses to the filing of the report of Mr. Sudetic, and I believe we've now received, I think, all of the Defence responses and I would ask the Chamber to granted us leave to reply, give us an extension of five working days until next Friday to file our reply, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, after a brief deliberation the Chamber is granting you five working days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, now that my colleague has raised this, the issue of deadlines, I don't want to say anything that will be premature, but since we're not in session tomorrow, and just this afternoon we have received two other large-scale motions from the OTP, one about tendering documents in relation to a protected person, I'm not sure if there is protection or not, so I dare not say the person's name. And the other motion is about a 92 bis witness, something to do with Vares. There's a third -- a smaller motion which is not as important, but these two large-scale motions, extensive motions, require a lot of preparation and analysis for us to be able to provide an adequate reply. Furthermore, you know that over the past couple of days we have been requesting deadline extensions since we are overburdened as we are with all the motions that already exist. You have granted us an extension to the 12th of July and we thank you for it. We want to clear our table, as it were, before we leave. This notwithstanding we still haven't managed to all sit down together as Defence teams and discuss what exactly we would do. My take on it is we will not be able to provide an answer, reply, within a reasonable time. I don't wish to tire you with it but I think we will have to request another extension in order to be able to submit our reply after the break. I think we are entitled to several days' break. If we don't ask for an extension to the end of July, that means we will have to be working throughout our summer break. This is a lot of work, and it also requires communication between the Defence teams. However, may we be given an opportunity to redefine this whole thing once we have managed to sit down together and look at the situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... Work as you can see. The Trial Chamber at times issues two or three rulings a day. It takes time to read them. There are filings by the Prosecution, at times two or three per day as well, which means that you really are snowed under. A heavy burden of motions, you have to prepare for cross-examination, you must prepare for the 92 bis phase. You must prepare your witnesses, which is really quite a heavy workload. I'm aware of that. Regarding your application on the three motions we'll have to discuss this, but I'm going to do this right now. Unless Mr. Stewart wants to say the same, or something along the same lines?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, if I was going to say the same, Your Honours, I wouldn't trouble Your Honours this evening. I'm going to say something different. Your Honours, it was just on the question of the 94 bis notice in relation to Mr. Sudetic. I just wanted to be clear because 94 bis (B) provides for a notice. Now, the Petkovic Defence notice was in slightly fuller terms than some of the others. Some of the others were just very brief notices with the points, and I just wanted to be clear, Your Honour that when the Prosecution have put in a reply that at that point, Your Honours would, with any submissions on counsel, review where we go from here. Because it's not like a full motion with a full response and then a full reply. The fact that it is a notice means that points are made which then may require more elaborate argument. So I just wanted to put down a marker, Your Honour, that I hope Your Honours wouldn't then simply be proceeding without any further consideration to make rulings on this, without considering whether there should be the opportunity for, for example, some oral submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. We were seized by the Prosecution of this notice under 94 bis (B). The Defence teams are free to reply, so I can't see why you're so concerned. You're free to reply. Either you comply or you agree to the motion, or you challenge it, because according to you it is not properly formulated under Rule 94 bis (B), and you would apply for the witness to be a viva voce witness. But it is up to you. You can realise --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I'm not making my point clearly enough, Your Honour. The Rule requires a notice from the Defence saying whether they admit or don't accept the report, whether they do want cross-examination, whether they challenge the qualifications and so on. And Your Honours will see in one or two cases, the notice takes the form, no, we don't accept it, yes, we do want to cross-examine. Just giving a very clear indication what the position is, what the Rule requires. So, Your Honours, it's clear that what the Defence teams have not on the whole done is attempt to set out the full submissions in the way that we normally do in response to a motion. Your Honour, I'm not asking for this all to be resolved this evening, I'm just asking for Your Honours to bear in mind that when the Prosecution are putting their reply, it may very well be that we're in a position where it won't be appropriate, with respect, for Your Honours simply to go straight on to a ruling without a further opportunity. I'm only asking that Your Honours don't do that without the opportunity to reconsider it in the future. But not at 3 minutes past 7.00 this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I know it's late, but in response, I do have to make a response to that, just so the record is clear -- just so the record is very clear, the Prosecution indeed made a filing, which is simply a notice, and I think was really all of one page. It simply says, "Attached please find the report which is hereby filed." Now in response to that, the Petkovic team in particular filed a six-page reply, so I don't think it was not -- it was not a non-reply. It was a six-page objection, extensively objecting to the receipt of the report. So with that clarification, we can address the matter further if and when the Chamber decides to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let's talk about next week. As you know, on Monday, the Prosecution does not have any witness available. As a result, we'll start that particular week on Monday -- on Tuesday, 9.00 a.m. On Wednesday we'll be sitting in the afternoon. And on Thursday in the morning. Now, with respect to the time for that witness, the witness who will testify during three days, the Prosecution says they need six hours, we'll consider the matter because we haven't time to do so. And you'll receive an e-mail tomorrow telling us what we think about this, but of course the Defence will have to work out how they will spread the time amongst themselves. We'll only intervene if you can't find an agreement. We'll let you know about the time tomorrow, a minimum of six hours for the Prosecution, a minimum of six hours for the Defence, but that's all I can say about the matter now. You'll be further informed and notified tomorrow. The witness has concluded his testimony. As a result, we won't sit tomorrow. Colonel, on behalf of my colleagues, I'd like to thank you for your contribution after having been called here to testify by the Prosecution. I wish you a safe trip home. We are going to conclude, and I'd like to apologise to the interpreters, because we -- it's a bit later than usual. So we'll reconvene on Tuesday at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 3rd day of July, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
